community.metaDescription: How FRAME works: who the photographers are, what an appreciation means, and how a new location is proposed and reviewed.
community.heading: Photographs,<break></break>and the people <accent>behind</accent> them.
community.lead: FRAME is a record of street photographs and of the real places they were made in. Everything on it was published by a member who holds the rights to their own work, and every location was reviewed by a person before it appeared on the map.

appreciation.title: What an appreciation means
appreciation.once: An appreciation is the only way to say something about a photograph on FRAME, and it counts once per member. Appreciating a frame a second time withdraws the first, so the number under an image is a count of people rather than a count of clicks.
appreciation.notForSale: Appreciations cannot be bought, promoted or transferred, and no amount of them changes how a photograph is moderated. The editor’s picks are chosen by editors, always carry that label, and are never paid for.
appreciation.trending: Trending orders photographs so that recent appreciations weigh more than old ones. That is the whole rule, and it is written on the <discover>Discover</discover> page beside the sort control, because a ranking nobody can explain is a ranking nobody should trust.

review.title: How a location is reviewed
review.proposeBody: A name, a city, a coordinate and a note about what makes it worth the walk. Up to {maxPerDay, plural, one {# proposal} other {# proposals}} a day, which is enough for a good afternoon and not enough to flood the queue.
review.checksBody: Duplicate candidates nearby, a coordinate that does not sit in the country it claims, an unusually coarse point. These are shown to a moderator as signals and never decide anything on their own.
review.decideBody: Approved, declined with a reason the member can read, or returned with a request for changes. Access and photography restrictions are only published when a moderator has recorded where the claim came from.
review.publishBody: An approved place is pinned to {publicPrecision}. Somewhere privacy-sensitive is coarsened to {reducedPrecision} and labelled as approximate, and some places carry no coordinate at all. GPS found in a photograph’s metadata is never published unless the member chooses to publish it.
review.guidelines: What will and will not be approved is set out in the <guidelines>community guidelines</guidelines>.

delete.heading: Delete your account
delete.whatGoes: Your profile, every photograph and its image files, your collections, the appreciation you have given, and any places you proposed that are still waiting are deleted.

Only its username remains, on the decisions you made.

file.heading: Choose the photograph
file.lead: One photograph per upload. {formats} files up to {size}, at least {width} by {height} pixels.
file.browseHint: or press Enter to browse your files
file.clientCheckNote: These two checks run in your browser, so they are a convenience rather than a control. FRAME reads the real contents of the file on the server after it arrives, and refuses anything that is not a photograph it can publish — whatever the file was named or said it was.
file.previewAlt: Preview of {fileName}, the photograph you have chosen to upload
file.exifRead: Read from the file: {facts}. You can change any of it later.
file.exifNone: This file carries no camera metadata. That is common and nothing is wrong — you can type the details in yourself.

exifGps.title: This file records where it was taken
exifGps.policy: This file contains the coordinates your camera recorded. FRAME will not publish them unless you choose to: leave this question alone and the position stays out of the photograph entirely. If you do publish a place, the point is shown as you submitted it — nobody posts in real time, and an exact point is what another photographer can actually use — unless a moderator judges the place sensitive, in which case it is coarsened or withheld. Camera metadata is also not a claim of authorship — it says which device wrote the file, not who holds the rights to the photograph.
exifGps.onFileStep: You will be asked about it on the place step, and nothing happens with it unless you choose it there.
exifGps.usedTitle: Using the position from the file
exifGps.usedBody: The coordinates below were copied from the file because you chose to use them. Edit them freely — they are a starting point, not a fact.
exifGps.declinedTitle: The position in the file stays out of this
exifGps.declinedBody: Nothing from the file’s position has been copied anywhere, and none of it will be stored.
exifGps.use: Use it to start a proposal

describe.heading: Describe the frame
describe.lead: A title, a category, and the alt text a screen reader will read aloud. The description is optional and is where the story behind the frame goes.
describe.titleHint: Up to {max, number} characters. This becomes the photograph's web address.
describe.categoryHint: One category per photograph. It decides which filters this frame appears under.
describe.altTextHint: This is what a screen-reader user hears instead of seeing the photograph, so describe what is in the frame rather than how it makes you feel. Between {min, number} and {max, number} characters — {count, number} so far.
describe.altTextPlaceholder: A woman crosses an empty street under a row of shuttered shopfronts, lit by a single vending machine.
describe.descriptionHint: Optional. How you found the frame, what you waited for, what you would do differently.
describe.descriptionPlaceholder: I had walked past this junction four nights running before the shutters and the rain lined up.

place.heading: Where was it made?
place.lead: A place is what turns a photograph into something another photographer can go and see for themselves. It is also somewhere real, so FRAME publishes it only after a person has looked at it, at the precision that person chooses.
place.modeLegend: How would you like to answer?
place.modeNoneDescription: Publish without a location. You can tell us where it was made later without re-uploading.
place.modeExistingDescription: Search the places already on the map and pick the one this frame was made at.
place.modeProposeDescription: Somewhere FRAME does not have yet. A moderator reads every proposal before it appears.
place.searchHint: Search by place, city or country. Two characters is enough to start.
place.searchNoResults: No approved place matches that. If FRAME does not have it yet, propose it instead.
place.searchResultCount: {count, plural, one {# place found.} other {# places found.}}
place.searchLegend: Choose the place this frame was made at
place.nameHint: What a photographer would call it, not a postal address.
place.countryCodeHint: Two letters, ISO 3166-1 — JP, DK, TH.
place.pointHint: Search by name, or click the map to drop a pin and drag it to the exact spot. The city, country and code fill themselves in from the point, and you can edit any of them. The two fields below follow the pin — use them if you have the coordinate from a GPS or from the camera.
place.searchByNameLabel: Search for the place by name
place.searchByNamePlaceholder: Wat Arun, Shibuya Crossing, Praça do Comércio
place.searchByNameHint: Finds the point on the map and fills in the city and country. Suggestions appear as you type, from three letters; Enter or the button searches at once.
place.searchByNameNone: Nothing found by that name. Drop a pin on the map instead, or try a nearby landmark.

place.pickerChosen: Pinned at {latitude}, {longitude}. Drag the pin to adjust it.
place.pickerCooperativeGesture: Hold ctrl or ⌘ and scroll to zoom the map
place.pickerCooperativeTouch: Use two fingers to move the map
place.noteHint: Optional. Access, opening hours, whether photography is restricted — anything a moderator should know before this goes on a public map.
place.checksIdle: Enter a latitude, a longitude and a country code and the coordinate checks run here as you type.
place.checksNone: The coordinate checks found nothing to flag. That is not the same as FRAME knowing this place exists — a moderator still reads the proposal.
place.signalOutOfRange: Coordinates fall outside the valid latitude/longitude range.
place.signalLowPrecision: Coordinates look like placeholder values (whole degrees or 0,0). Ask for a precise point.
place.signalCountryMismatch: The point does not fall within the bounding box of {countryCode}.
place.signalCountryUnknown: No bounding box on file for {countryCode}, so the country could not be cross-checked.
place.signalPossibleDuplicate: Within {metres, number} m of an existing location.
place.proposalNoticeTitle: What happens to a proposed place
place.proposalNoticeBody: Your proposal is queued for a moderator and does not appear on the map until one approves it. Your photograph does not wait for that: it publishes as soon as the automated checks clear it, with the place marked pending, and is credited to the location once it is approved.
place.proposalNoticePrecision: A published point is shown as submitted unless a moderator marks the place as sensitive, when it is coarsened — to {precision} or to about a kilometre — or withheld. Two proposals within {radius, number} m of each other are flagged as possible duplicates for a person to compare.
place.noneChosen: Publishing without a place is a perfectly good answer. Street photographs of somebody’s street are often better off without a pin on them.

gear.heading: Camera and lens
gear.lead: All optional. Filling it in is what makes the gear filters on Discover useful to somebody deciding what to carry.
gear.noneRead: This file recorded no camera or lens, so nothing has been filled in. Type what you used, or leave it blank.
gear.lensBrandHint: Leave blank for a fixed lens, or if it is the same as the camera.
gear.note: If your camera is not one FRAME already lists, what you type is kept exactly as you wrote it. Nobody is asked to pretend they shot something else.
gear.filmHint: A scan carries no camera record, so name the camera above. A reviewer sees the claim beside the missing record. Phone photographs are refused either way.

settings.heading: Exposure and editing
settings.lead: How the frame was exposed, and what you did to it afterwards. All optional, and all of it useful to somebody trying to work out how a photograph was made.
settings.noneRead: This file recorded no exposure settings, so nothing has been filled in. Type what you remember, or leave it blank — a guess written as a fact is worse than a gap.
settings.focalLengthHint: In millimetres, as written on the lens.
settings.apertureHint: The f-number alone — 2 for f/2, 5.6 for f/5.6.
settings.shutterSpeedHint: Write it as 1/250 below a second, or as 4s at or above one.
settings.isoHint: The sensitivity the camera was set to.
settings.editingSoftwareHint: Lightroom, Capture One, Darktable, the camera's own film simulation — whatever you used.
settings.editingNotesHint: What you changed and why. This is the part other photographers read most closely.
settings.editingNotesPlaceholder: Lifted the shadows about a stop, pulled the greens out of the fluorescent light, no crop.
settings.captureDateNone: This file does not say when it was taken, so there is no date to publish or withhold. The date FRAME shows on the photograph is the day it was published.
settings.captureDateBody: Your camera recorded this frame as taken on {date}. A capture date can place a person somewhere on a particular evening, so FRAME leaves it out unless you ask for it. The camera carries no time zone, so the date is read as your camera’s own clock.
settings.captureDateDescription: Leave this unticked and the date stays off the photograph and out of its record.

review.heading: Check it over
review.lead: This is everything FRAME is about to store. Nothing has been uploaded yet, so a change here costs you nothing.
review.valueDimensions: {width} × {height} pixels, as the file reports them
review.valueProposalStatus: Queued for a moderator. Your photograph publishes once the automated checks clear it; the place appears once it is approved.
review.valueNoPlace: None. The photograph publishes without a location, and you can add one later without re-uploading.
review.valueCaptureDateWithheld: Withheld. The file records a date and you chose not to publish it.
review.valueGpsUsed: The file records a position and you used it to start your proposal. It is stored with your consent recorded against it, and it is never published as an exact point.
review.valueGpsDeclined: The file records a position. You chose to leave it out, so it is not stored.
review.previewAltFallback: The photograph you have chosen. You have not written alt text for it yet.
review.rightsIntro: FRAME publishes photographs on the strength of this one statement, so it is worth reading rather than skipping.
review.rightsAuthor: You are the photographer, or you hold written permission from the photographer to publish this work.
review.rightsCopyright: You keep your copyright. Publishing here transfers nothing.
review.rightsLicence: You grant FRAME only the licence it needs to display the work on the platform and to promote the platform with it — nothing wider.
review.rightsCommercial: Any commercial or advertising use needs separate permission from you, asked for and agreed each time.
review.rightsTerms: The full terms are at <link>the copyright policy</link>.
review.rightsConfirm: I am the photographer or hold permission to publish this work, and I grant FRAME the licence described above.
review.rightsConfirmDescription: FRAME records the moment you tick this and checks it again on the server before anything is published.
review.twoThingsBody: Your photograph, which publishes as soon as the automated checks clear it, and your proposed place, which waits for a moderator. A published point is shown as submitted unless the moderator decides the place is sensitive.

submit.heading: Send it
submit.lead: {fileName}, {size}, going to storage and then through the server's own checks.
submit.noFile: No file is attached to this upload.
submit.notConfiguredTitle: Nothing will be uploaded from this deployment
submit.notConfiguredBody: This copy of FRAME cannot accept a photograph: it has no database, or the storage provider it was pointed at is missing its credentials. The notice at the top of this page names exactly what is absent. Either way there is nowhere for the file to go, so the wizard is here in full only as a design review.
submit.notConfiguredDocs: Submitting will refuse and repeat that explanation rather than show you a success that did not happen. The variables that turn uploads on are listed in docs/ENVIRONMENT.md.
submit.stageDraftDetail: FRAME creates the draft that will own the file, under your account.
submit.stageGrantDetail: The server works out where the file goes and issues a grant for that one object, that one format and that one size. Nothing about the destination is chosen by this browser.
submit.stageUploadDetail: The bytes go straight to storage rather than through FRAME.
submit.stageProcessDetail: The server decodes the file that actually arrived, refuses anything that is not a photograph it can publish, then builds the sizes the site serves and strips every tag from each of them.
submit.stagePublishDetail: Your declaration is recorded and an automated check looks at the image. If it is clear, the photograph is published at once; if not, a moderator looks first.
submit.stagePlaceDetail: Your proposal goes to a moderator. Your photograph does not wait for it.
submit.statusUnderReview: Uploaded and waiting on a moderator.
submit.guidanceNotConfigured: Nothing was uploaded and nothing was saved. This is a configuration gap in the deployment, not something your file did wrong.
submit.guidanceUnauthenticated: Your session has ended. Sign in again in another tab and press submit here — everything you have entered is still on this page, as long as you do not reload it.

submit.outcomePublishedBody: Your photograph is live. It passed the automated checks, the sizes FRAME serves have been generated from it with every tag stripped, and your original file has been deleted rather than kept.

nav.note: All four are working drafts kept in step with the product. They are written in the same repository as the code so that a policy and the behaviour it describes cannot drift apart unnoticed.

draft.title: A starting draft, and not legal advice
draft.body: FRAME is a project in development. This document was drafted alongside the software so that what it says matches what the software does, but it is not legal advice, no lawyer has reviewed it, and it needs that review before FRAME is opened to the public.

translation.title: A translation for convenience; the English version governs
translation.body: This page is a translation provided for your convenience. If anything in it conflicts with <english>the English version of this document</english>, the English version governs.
translation.footer: This page is a translation. Where it differs from <english>the English version</english>, the English version is the one that applies.

shell.defect: Something in this document that does not match how FRAME behaves is a defect in the document. Report it the same way you would report anything else, and it will be corrected here rather than explained away.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.description: Who may use FRAME, what members may publish, and what happens when they do not.
terms.summary: These terms cover who may hold an account, what may be published, what happens when something is published that should not have been, and the limits of what FRAME promises while it is still being built.

privacy.title: Privacy notice
privacy.description: What FRAME records, what it publishes, what it refuses to publish, and who else handles it.
privacy.summary: FRAME collects an email address, whatever you choose to write on your profile, the photographs you upload, and the records needed to keep appreciation and moderation honest. It publishes far less than it holds, and it never publishes a coordinate you did not choose to publish.

copyright.title: Copyright and takedown
copyright.description: The photographer keeps the copyright. What licence uploading grants, and how an infringement claim is handled.
copyright.summary: You keep the copyright in everything you publish here. FRAME takes only the narrow licence it needs to show your work on FRAME, and this page sets out how a claim that somebody has published work that is not theirs is handled.

guidelines.title: Community guidelines
guidelines.description: What belongs on FRAME, how to photograph people in public, which places not to pin, and how appreciation is kept honest.
guidelines.summary: FRAME works because photographers treat the people in their frames, the places they pin and each other’s work carefully. These are the expectations that go with holding an account, written as plainly as they can be.

eligibility.heading: Who may use FRAME
eligibility.p1: Anyone may read FRAME. Browsing photographs, places and profiles needs no account and no sign-in.
eligibility.p2: An account is for people aged 16 or over, or the local minimum age for consenting to online services where that is higher. One account per person. An account is personal, is not transferable, and the password on it is yours to keep to yourself.
eligibility.p3: FRAME may decline to create an account, and may close one, for the reasons set out under suspension below.

acceptableUse.heading: Acceptable use
acceptableUse.intro: FRAME is a community archive of street photography. Use it for that. In particular, do not:

list.notYourWork: publish a photograph you did not make, or that you do not have the rights and permissions to publish;
list.unlawful: publish anything unlawful, anything that harasses or endangers a person, or anything that sexualises a child;
list.unsafePin: pin a photograph to a private home or to a place where a published coordinate puts somebody at risk, which the <guidelines>community guidelines</guidelines> set out in detail;
list.manipulation: inflate appreciation with second accounts, reciprocal arrangements or automation, or interfere with the ordering of what other people see;
list.scraping: scrape the site, work around a rate limit, or try to reach another member’s drafts, private collections, email address or reports;
list.falseReports: file reports you do not believe, which wastes the time a real one needs.

acceptableUse.limits: Uploads are also bounded technically: at most {maxFileSize} per file, at least {minWidth, number} by {minHeight, number} pixels, JPEG, PNG, WebP or AVIF, and up to {maxPerDay, plural, one {# photograph} other {# photographs}} a day. Those limits exist to keep one account from running up everybody’s costs, not to judge your work.

yourWork.heading: Your work, and your responsibility for it
yourWork.p1: You keep the copyright in every photograph you upload. What uploading grants FRAME, and what it does not, is set out in the <copyright>copyright notice</copyright>.
yourWork.confirmIntro: By publishing a photograph on FRAME you confirm three things:

list.permission: you have whatever permission the law where you were standing requires from a recognisable person in the frame, or from the owner of a private property;
list.noBreach: publishing it breaks no contract, court order or embargo you are subject to.

yourWork.exif: FRAME reads the EXIF in a file to fill in the camera, the lens and the settings for you. That is a convenience and nothing more: EXIF says which camera produced a file, not who holds the copyright in the photograph, and FRAME does not treat it as evidence of ownership either way. A file with no EXIF at all is published on the same terms.
yourWork.altText: Alt text is required on every photograph because a published image without it is not published to everybody. Write what is in the frame.
yourWork.responsibility: You remain responsible for what you publish. FRAME is the venue, not the author, and a claim about a photograph is answered by the person who uploaded it.

suspension.heading: Suspension and termination
suspension.p1: You can delete your account whenever you like. What that removes, and what survives it, is described in the <privacy>privacy notice</privacy>.
suspension.intro: FRAME may suspend an account where there is:

list.credibleClaim: a credible claim that a photograph on it is not the uploader’s work;
list.repeatedDisregard: repeated disregard of the community guidelines after being told;
list.manipulation: manipulation of appreciation or of the ordering of the galleries;
list.harassment: harassment of another member, or of a person in a photograph.

suspension.recorded: A suspension is recorded with a reason and the reason is shown to the account it concerns. A suspended account can still read FRAME but cannot publish, appreciate, submit a place or change a collection. Suspension is not deletion: the work is hidden, not destroyed, while the matter is settled.
suspension.revisited: Every one of those decisions is made by a person and can be revisited by a person. If a decision about your account was wrong, say so and it will be looked at again.
suspension.record: The record of a moderation decision is kept even after the photograph or the account it concerned has gone, because a record of why something was removed is what stops the same dispute reopening from the beginning.

liability.heading: Limitation of liability
liability.asIs: FRAME is provided as it is. While the project is in development it may be unavailable without notice, may lose data, and may change in ways that are not backwards compatible. Keep your own copies of your photographs.
liability.notes: The shooting notes, access notes and restrictions attached to a place are written by members and checked by moderators against a recorded source. They are not a guarantee. Whether a place is safe to stand in, open to the public, or legal to photograph is for you to establish locally before you go, and it can change between the note being written and your arriving.
liability.limits: To the extent the law allows, FRAME is not liable for indirect or consequential loss arising from use of the site, including lost work, lost income or a journey made on the strength of a location note. Nothing here limits liability that cannot lawfully be limited, including liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence, or for fraud.
liability.outstanding: The operating entity, the governing law and the forum for a dispute are not yet settled and must be named here before FRAME is launched. Until then this document describes intent, not an enforceable agreement.

changes.heading: Changes to these terms
changes.p1: These terms will change as the product does, and the date at the top of this page records when they were last read through.
changes.p2: A change that materially affects what members may do, or what FRAME may do with their work, will be announced in the interface before it takes effect rather than quietly published. Continuing to use FRAME after that notice means accepting the change; if you would rather not, you can remove your work and close your account.
changes.p3: The current version always lives at this address. There is no separate paper copy that says something different.

whatIsCollected.heading: What is collected
whatIsCollected.intro: Only what the site needs in order to work:

list.email: An email address, so an account can be recovered and verified. The password itself is never stored; the authentication provider holds a hash of it and FRAME never sees the original.
list.signIn: If you sign in with Google, Apple, Facebook or X: the name and email address that provider shares, and its identifier for your account there. FRAME never receives your password for that provider, and an account made this way has no FRAME password at all. Apple can hide your real address behind a relay address; FRAME keeps whichever address Apple sends.
list.profile: The profile fields you write: username, display name, avatar, biography, where you are based, a website, and the gear you choose to list. Every one of them is free text you decide to enter, and every one of them is optional except the username and display name.
list.photographs: The photographs you upload and the EXIF inside them: camera and lens, focal length, aperture, shutter speed, ISO, the capture date and, where the camera recorded one, a GPS coordinate.
list.appreciation: Appreciation records: which account appreciated which photograph. Appreciation is one per member, and that cannot be enforced without keeping the record of who it was.
list.reports: Reports: the thing reported, the reason chosen, any note written, and the reporting account where the reporter was signed in.
list.placeSubmissions: Place submissions: the name, city, country, coordinate and note proposed for a new location.
list.rateLimits: Rate-limit counters, keyed to the account taking the action.

whatIsCollected.notCollected: Not collected: an advertising identifier, a behavioural profile, cross-site tracking, or a record of what anyone searches for. FRAME has no analytics vendor embedded in it.

whatIsPublished.heading: What is published, and what is not
whatIsPublished.published: Published, meaning visible to anyone including people with no account: your display name, username and avatar; your biography, based-in line, website and listed gear; the month you joined; the photographs you have published, with their titles, alt text, descriptions, categories and capture settings; the places you submitted that were approved; your public collections; and the appreciation count on each photograph.
whatIsPublished.notPublished: Not published: your email address; the exact day you joined, which is why a profile shows a month only; your drafts and anything still processing; your private collections; which photographs you appreciated, as distinct from the totals; the reports you filed and the fact that you filed them; and your rate-limit counters.
whatIsPublished.removal: A photograph you remove, or that a moderator removes, stops being served immediately. Caches and other people’s browsers may hold a copy for a short while afterwards, which is a property of the web rather than a decision FRAME makes.

exifAndPlace.heading: EXIF, and the place a photograph was made
exifAndPlace.p1: EXIF is read in your browser as you choose a file, so the upload form can offer the camera and the settings back to you instead of asking you to type them. You can change or clear any of it before publishing.
exifAndPlace.gps: A GPS coordinate found in EXIF is never published automatically. It is used for one purpose: to ask whether you want to pin the photograph to a place. If you do not answer, nothing is pinned. A coordinate that stays in the file you uploaded is not served to anyone, because what FRAME serves are generated derivatives with the metadata stripped out.
exifAndPlace.precision: Where you do publish a place, the point is shown as you submitted it: nobody posts in real time, and an exact point is what another photographer can actually use. A moderator may instead publish it coarsened — to {publicUnit, select, km {about {publicValue, number} km} other {about {publicValue, number} m}}, or for a privacy-sensitive place to {reducedUnit, select, km {about {reducedValue, number} km} other {about {reducedValue, number} m}} — and where even that would be unsafe no coordinate is published at all. The map and the page both say when a point is deliberately approximate, and a moderator can change the precision of a published place at any time.
exifAndPlace.reduction: Precision is only ever reduced, never widened: a coarsened point stays coarsened, and there is no stored copy of the finer value that a later change could expose. If you published a place and now regret it, ask and it will be coarsened or removed.

ipAddresses.heading: Why an IP address is not treated as identity
ipAddresses.p1: An IP address identifies a connection at a moment, not a person. It is shared by everyone in a household, an office, a university or a café, it is shared at much larger scale by mobile carriers, and it changes — sometimes several times a day.
ipAddresses.p2: So FRAME keys its limits and its records to an account rather than to an address. Treating an address as a person gets it wrong in both directions: a crowded café is throttled as though it were one very busy member, while somebody determined to abuse the site only has to reconnect.
ipAddresses.p3: The exceptions are the requests that arrive before a session exists — signing up, signing in, asking for a password reset — where the limit can only be applied to the attempt itself. Those counters are short-lived and are not used to build a profile.
ipAddresses.p4: A hosting provider records the IP address of every request as part of serving it. That is true of any website. FRAME does not read those logs to identify a member, does not join them to account records, and does not use them for anything other than keeping the service running.

retention.heading: How long things are kept

list.account: Account and profile: for as long as the account exists.
list.photographs: Published photographs and their generated sizes: until you remove them, or until the account is deleted.
list.drafts: Drafts: until you publish or discard them. A draft that is never finished is still yours.
list.appreciation: Appreciation records: while both the account and the photograph exist.
list.reports: Reports and moderation decisions: kept after the thing they concerned has gone, because the reason something was removed is the only answer to the same claim arriving twice. They are attached to the moderator who decided, not to the person who reported.
list.rateLimits: Rate-limit counters: hours, not months. They are cleaned up as they expire.

retention.backups: Backups will hold a copy of deleted content for a period after deletion. A specific retention window for backups has to be set, and stated here, before launch.

accessAndDeletion.heading: Access, correction and deletion
accessAndDeletion.p1: Most of this you can do yourself, from Settings and from your collections: edit your display name, profile picture, biography, location, website and gear; replace a username that was chosen for you, once; make a collection private, or delete it; and delete the account outright. One thing cannot be done yourself yet: a published photograph cannot be withdrawn on its own: report it to have a moderator take it down, or delete the account, which removes every one.
accessAndDeletion.p2: Deleting an account removes the profile, every photograph and the image files generated from it, the collections, the appreciation the account gave, and any place it proposed that is still waiting. Reports it filed and places that were approved are kept with the account’s name removed, because other people’s decisions rest on them; moderation decisions likewise keep their content with the account reference removed wherever that is possible, for the reason above. One kind of account cannot be erased: one that has made moderation decisions, because an audit trail cannot be left without an author. Such an account is emptied instead — its photographs, collections, appreciation and profile details deleted, its role removed — and closed: hidden from the site and unable to sign in, with only its username left on the decisions it made. That is worth knowing before anybody is made a moderator.
accessAndDeletion.p3: You can ask for a copy of what is held about you, and for a correction of anything that is wrong. The contact route for those requests, and the supervisory authority a complaint can be taken to, must be named here before launch.

thirdParties.heading: Who else handles this
thirdParties.intro: FRAME is a small application standing on five services, and on a sixth only if you choose it:

list.database: The database and authentication provider (Supabase, Postgres and its auth service) holds accounts, profiles, photographs, appreciation, reports and the email address and password hash.
list.storage: The image storage provider (Supabase Storage, or Cloudflare R2 where that is configured instead) holds the sizes generated from your upload. The file you uploaded is deleted as soon as those sizes exist, so its EXIF data — including any position it recorded — is not kept.
list.contentCheck: The automated content check (Google Cloud Vision SafeSearch) receives one copy of each uploaded photograph — the display size FRAME generated, with every tag removed — and answers how likely it is to be adult, violent or graphic. Google processes it to give that answer and nothing else; FRAME keeps only the answer, which moderators can see.
list.tiles: The map tile provider supplies the style and tiles for the map. Your browser requests those tiles directly, so that provider sees the request, including your IP address, the way any website you visit does. FRAME ships with no tile provider configured and deliberately falls back to no map rather than to somebody’s evaluation server.
list.hosting: The hosting provider runs the application and logs requests as described above.
list.signIn: A sign-in provider — Google, Apple, Meta for Facebook, or X — only if you choose to sign in with one. That provider learns that you signed in to FRAME, and when. How to disconnect it is set out under “Signing in with another account”.
list.translation: The translation provider (Google Cloud Translation) receives the words you write — a photograph’s title, description and alt text, a comment, a place’s name and description, a biography — and returns them in the other of FRAME’s two languages, so a reader who does not share your language can still read them. Only text that is already published is sent: a draft, and an upload still waiting for a moderator, never leave FRAME. Google processes the text to produce that translation and nothing else. A translation is always labelled as automatic, and the words as you wrote them are always one click away.

thirdParties.demo: A deployment with no database configured shows a bundled sample dataset instead, and says so on every page. The sample photographs in that mode are served from Unsplash under the Unsplash licence and describe nobody real.
thirdParties.outstanding: Each of those providers needs to be named specifically, with a data-processing agreement in place, before FRAME handles anybody’s real data. See <terms>the terms</terms> for what is still outstanding.

signInProviders.heading: Signing in with another account
signInProviders.p1: Signing in with Google, Apple, Facebook or X is optional: an email address and a password work everywhere on FRAME. If you use a provider, FRAME asks it for your name and email address and nothing more, and keeps only what is listed under “What is collected”.
signInProviders.disconnect: You can stop a provider sharing anything further with FRAME at any time, from that provider’s own account settings. At the time of writing they are here:

list.google: Google: your Google Account → Security → Your connections to third-party apps and services → FRAME.
list.apple: Apple: on an iPhone, Settings → your name → Sign-In & Security → Sign in with Apple → FRAME; on the web, account.apple.com → Sign-In and Security → Sign in with Apple.
list.facebook: Facebook: Settings & privacy → Settings → Apps and websites → FRAME → Remove.
list.twitter: X: Settings and privacy → Security and account access → Apps and sessions → Connected apps → FRAME → Revoke app permissions.

signInProviders.deletion: Disconnecting stops new information arriving. It does not delete your FRAME account or anything you published on it: deleting the account and its data is done as set out under “Access, correction and deletion”.

ownership.heading: The photographer keeps the copyright
ownership.p1: Uploading a photograph to FRAME transfers nothing. You made it, you own it, and you can license it to whoever you like on whatever terms you like, including terms FRAME knows nothing about.
ownership.p2: Every photograph is shown with its photographer’s name and a link to their profile, and the footer of every page says that FRAME licenses nothing on anyone’s behalf. That is not decoration: it is the whole arrangement.

licence.heading: The licence you grant FRAME
licence.intro: Publishing a photograph grants FRAME a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free licence, for as long as the photograph is on FRAME, to do four things and no more:

list.derivatives: generate the smaller sizes needed to show it without sending a full-resolution original to every visitor;
list.display: display it on FRAME’s own pages — the galleries, the map, a location page, a profile, a collection — with your credit;
list.editorial: feature it in FRAME’s own editorial promotion of FRAME, such as an editor’s pick or a post about a photograph that is on the site, again with your credit.

licence.exclusions: That licence does not include sublicensing your work to a third party, selling it, offering it as stock, printing it for sale, using it in paid advertising, or using it to train a machine-learning model. None of those are covered, and none of them will be added by amending this page quietly.
licence.ends: Removing the photograph ends the licence. Already-generated sizes are deleted with it; anything already printed on paper obviously cannot be recalled, which is why the promotional use above is deliberately narrow.

commercialUse.heading: Commercial and advertising use needs separate permission
commercialUse.p1: Any use beyond the four above is a separate agreement between you and whoever wants it. That includes advertising, merchandise, editorial use by a publication, print sales and licensing to a brand, whether the request reaches you through FRAME or not.
commercialUse.p2: Where someone contacts FRAME wanting to license a photograph, they are given the photographer’s profile and nothing else. FRAME does not negotiate on your behalf, does not take a cut, and does not pass on your email address without asking you first.

takedown.heading: Reporting an infringement
takedown.intro: If a photograph on FRAME is yours and was published by somebody else, report it with the reason {reasonNotMine} or {reasonCopyright}, and include the following. A complaint missing any of it cannot be acted on, and will be returned saying which part is missing.

list.address: The address of the photograph on FRAME.
list.work: Identification of the work you say it infringes: a link to where you published it, or a copy, or enough description to identify it unambiguously.
list.relationship: Your relationship to that work — the photographer, the rights holder, or an agent.
list.contact: Your name and an address we can reply to.
list.goodFaith: A statement that you believe in good faith that the use on FRAME is not authorised.
list.accuracy: A statement that what you have said is accurate.

takedown.nextIntro: What happens next, and roughly when:

steps.acknowledge: Within two working days the complaint is acknowledged and read by a moderator.
steps.hidden: Where the claim is on its face valid, the photograph is hidden while it is examined. Hiding it is a precaution, not a finding: it means nobody is harmed further while the question is open.
steps.uploaderTold: Within five working days the uploader is told what has been claimed, and by whom to the extent they need in order to answer it. They have ten working days to respond.
steps.decision: A decision is recorded with a reason and both sides are told what it was. If the claim is upheld the photograph stays down. If it is not, the photograph comes back and the report is closed as dismissed.

takedown.timings: Those timings are the intent of a project with a small moderation team, not a contractual guarantee, and they will be revised here if they turn out to be unrealistic rather than quietly missed.

counterNotice.heading: If your photograph was removed and the claim was wrong
counterNotice.p1: You can answer a claim. A counter-notice needs the address of the photograph, an explanation of why you have the right to publish it, your name and a contact address, and a statement that what you have said is accurate.
counterNotice.p2: Where the answer is credible the photograph is restored and the complainant is told, so that they can take the matter further through a court if they still believe they are right. FRAME is not in a position to decide who owns a photograph: where two accounts both claim the same work and neither will move, the photograph stays down until they settle it between themselves or somebody with the authority to decide does.
counterNotice.p3: Filing a claim or a counter-notice you know to be false is grounds for closing the account, and in several jurisdictions is an offence in its own right.

repeatInfringement.heading: Repeat infringement
repeatInfringement.intro: Upheld claims are counted against the account they were upheld against.

steps.first: A first upheld claim: the photograph is removed and the member is told why.
steps.second: A second: uploading is suspended while the account is reviewed, and every other photograph on it is checked.
steps.third: A third: the account is closed.

repeatInfringement.notCounted: Claims that were withdrawn, dismissed or answered successfully are not counted. Deleting a photograph and uploading it again does not reset the count, and neither does opening a second account — an account opened to continue after a closure is closed as well.

similarityMatching.heading: A similarity match is a signal, never a finding
similarityMatching.p1: FRAME computes a perceptual fingerprint of each upload and shows a moderator when a new photograph closely resembles one already on the site. That check is useful and it is also close to blind: it cannot tell which of two uploads was made first, cannot tell a crop from a copy, and cannot tell a photographer re-uploading their own work from somebody taking it.
similarityMatching.p2: So it never removes anything by itself. It puts a pair in front of a person, who then has to do the actual work of establishing who made the photograph. The same is true of the other automated signals: a file with no EXIF is not evidence of theft, because exporting software strips EXIF as a matter of routine, and a burst of uploads is not evidence of anything except enthusiasm.
similarityMatching.p3: Those signals are shown in the moderation queue labelled as signals, with their severity, precisely so that nobody mistakes one for a conclusion. The <guidelines>community guidelines</guidelines> describe the rest of what moderators look at.

whatBelongs.heading: What belongs on FRAME
whatBelongs.categories: Photographs made in public places, in the six categories the site is built around: {categories}. A frame that would sit comfortably in any of those belongs here.
whatBelongs.posting: Post your own work, once. Write alt text that says what is in the frame rather than what it means. Where you know the place, say something useful about standing there: the hour the light works, the side of the street to wait on, whether a tripod will get you stopped.

list.notYourWork: work you did not make, however freely it was available elsewhere;
list.generated: generated images presented as photographs — if a frame was made by a model rather than a camera, this is not the place for it;
list.composites: composites assembled from several moments and presented as one. Processing a frame is photography; building a scene that never existed and captioning it with a street corner is not;
list.humiliation: anything whose point is a person’s humiliation, and anything published to settle a score with somebody in it.

whatBelongs.bounds: The technical bounds, for completeness: at most {maxFileSize} per file, at least {minWidth, number} by {minHeight, number} pixels, and up to {maxPerDay, plural, one {# photograph} other {# photographs}} a day.

people.heading: Consent and dignity when photographing people
people.p1: In much of the world it is lawful to photograph people in a public place. Lawful and decent are not the same question, and street photography lives in the gap between them.
people.p2: The test worth applying before publishing is simple: would the person recognise themselves as the subject of a photograph, or as its target? Do not publish a frame whose only content is somebody’s distress, poverty, disability, intoxication, illness or grief. A sleeping rough-sleeper is not a composition.
people.p3: Children need more care than adults, not less. Avoid publishing an identifiable child without the agreement of whoever is responsible for them.
people.p4: If someone in a photograph asks you to take it down, take it down. You do not have to agree that they are right, and you do not have to explain yourself; removing it costs you one frame.
people.p5: Several countries require consent for publication regardless of where the photograph was taken — France and Germany among them. Publishing is your decision and the law that applies to it is yours to know.

places.heading: Places not to pin
places.p1: A pin is an invitation. It tells strangers that something worth photographing is here and that they should come and stand in it. Most of the time that is the best thing about the site. Sometimes it is the reason not to add one.

list.home: a private home, including your own if anybody else lives there or next door to it;
list.sensitive: a shelter, a refuge, a clinic, a school, a place of worship under threat, or anywhere a published coordinate increases the risk to the people who use it;
list.dangerous: a place where standing there is dangerous or unlawful — a rooftop, a tunnel, a live railway, a restricted site. Marking it as a photographic location sends somebody else there after you.

places.sensitive: Where a place is genuinely sensitive but worth knowing about, pin the street or the district rather than the doorway. A moderator reviews every place before it is published and can coarsen or withhold its point, then or later; the <privacy>privacy notice</privacy> sets out the precisions involved.

appreciation.heading: Appreciation is one per member
appreciation.p1: Appreciation is a single mark of respect from one member to one photograph. It is not a score you can stack, and it cannot be given twice by the same account.
appreciation.p2: So: no second accounts, no arrangements to appreciate each other’s work in bulk, no scripts. Both sides of a swap are treated the same way, because both sides knew.
appreciation.trending: This matters more than it might sound. Appreciation feeds the trending order, where recent appreciation counts for more than old — the weight halves roughly every {halfLife, plural, one {# hour} other {# hours}}. Manipulating it does not just flatter one photograph; it decides what every visitor to the site is shown next.
appreciation.correction: Where manipulation is found the counts are corrected and the accounts involved are suspended. Correcting a count is not a punishment, it is an accounting fix: a number on this site is supposed to mean what it says.

accuracy.heading: Location accuracy, and how to report an error
accuracy.p1: A place entry is only worth having if it is right. Use the name people actually use for it, the city and country it is in, and a coordinate you are confident about rather than one you guessed from memory.
accuracy.checks: Submissions are reviewed before they appear. Automated checks look for a coordinate outside its stated country, a point within {radius, plural, one {# metre} other {# metres}} of an existing place, suspiciously round coordinates and a few other patterns. Those checks produce signals for a moderator to read and never a decision — a duplicate flag on two genuinely different doorways is exactly the sort of thing a person has to settle.
accuracy.reporting: If a published place is wrong, report it with the reason {reasonWrongLocation} and say what is wrong in the note: the corrected name, the right side of the street, the coordinate that should be there. A correction is far more useful than a removal, and much more likely to be acted on quickly.
accuracy.restrictions: Access notes and restrictions — permits, opening hours, a tripod ban, a fee — are only shown when a moderator has recorded where the claim came from. A restriction note nobody can source is worse than none at all, because it either sends people away from somewhere open or walks them into somewhere closed.

editorialPicks.heading: Editorial picks are never sold
editorialPicks.p1: An editor’s pick is chosen by a person at FRAME because they think the photograph deserves to be seen. It is always labelled as a pick, it is never paid for, and it is never traded for anything — not money, not reciprocal promotion, not a favour.
editorialPicks.p2: There is no promoted placement on FRAME, no paid position in the trending order and no sponsored collection. The orderings the galleries offer are described in the interface, including what each one actually sorts by, so that nobody has to guess whether a position was bought.
editorialPicks.p3: If that ever changes, the change will be labelled plainly as advertising and announced before it happens. A site that shows other people’s work has nothing to sell except whether it can be believed.

meta.title: Search
meta.description: Search FRAME for places, the photographs pinned to them and the photographers who made them.

search.heading: Find a place, a frame, a <accent>photographer.</accent>
search.scope: Search matches place names, cities and countries, and photographer names and usernames — not photograph titles, and never the content of the photographs themselves.

form.label: Search FRAME
form.placeholder: A city, a place or a photographer

prompt.heading: Start with a city
prompt.body: A city name finds the places photographers have pinned there and the frames they brought back from them. These are starting points rather than popular searches: FRAME keeps no record of what anyone searches for.
prompt.elsewhere: Or browse <discover>Discover</discover>, open the <map>map</map> or read the <locations>location index</locations>.

photographs.empty: No published photograph is pinned to a place matching “{query}”.

places.empty: No approved location matches those words yet.

people.label: Photographers
people.empty: No photographer name or username matches those words. Names are matched as written, so a partial surname works better than a full one spelled differently.

empty.title: Nothing matches “{query}”
empty.body: No place name, city, country or photographer name matched those words. A shorter search, or just the city, usually finds more.

route.title: This page could not be loaded
route.description: Something failed on the server while building this page. Nothing you did caused it and nothing was saved or changed. Trying again often works, because a failed read is frequently a transient one.
route.reference: Quote this reference if you report it: {digest}

notFound.title: Nothing at this address.
notFound.lead: The page you asked for is not here. That is usually one of four things.

reasons.mistyped: The address was mistyped, or the link that brought you here was built by hand.
reasons.removed: The photographer removed the photograph, or a moderator removed it after a report.
reasons.pending: The location has been submitted but not approved yet, so it has no public page.
reasons.private: A collection that used to be public has been made private by its owner.

notFound.searchHint: If you were looking for something in particular, searching for the place or the photographer by name is usually quicker than guessing a URL. <link>Search FRAME</link>.

series.metaDescription: {count} photographs by {name}, with the words around them.
series.colophon: Every photograph in this series is the work and copyright of {name}. It was written on FRAME from frames published here.

profile.title: Photo series
